appellations.name: Chassagne-Montrachet premier cru Les Rebichets
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay (Pinot Blanc permitted); Pinot Noir for the rarer reds
appellations.summary: Les Rebichets is a 4.7 ha part of the Clos Saint-Jean umbrella, above the village.
appellations.terroir: East-southeast-facing at 255 to 270 m, gentle slope, stony limestone-clay. On the map it lies below Clos Saint-Jean, above Chassagne and beside Les Vergers and Les Murées.
appellations.nerd_note: It may be sold under its own name or as Clos Saint-Jean.

appellations.name: Chassagne-Montrachet premier cru Les Vergers
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay (Pinot Blanc permitted); Pinot Noir for the rarer reds
appellations.summary:
Les Vergers ('the orchards') is a 9.5 ha premier cru north of the village, toward Saint-Aubin, and an umbrella for Les Pasquelles and Petingeret. Its whites are fine and mineral, among the best of the northern Chassagne premier crus.

Les Chenevottes lies below and Les Chaumées above. Niellon's and Ramonet's versions show the elegant, mineral side of Chassagne.
appellations.terroir: East-facing at 245 to 270 m, gentle slope, stony limestone-clay.
appellations.nerd_note: It continues into Saint-Aubin's Pitangeret across the commune line.

appellations.name: Chassagne-Montrachet premier cru Morgeot
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay (Pinot Blanc permitted); Pinot Noir for the rarer reds
appellations.summary:
Morgeot is the great southern premier cru of Chassagne-Montrachet and, as an umbrella name, the largest premier cru area of the commune: the INAO delimitation covers 56.4 ha, and wines from about twenty lieux-dits (Les Petits Clos, Les Grands Clos, Tête du Clos, La Boudriotte, Les Brussonnes, Vigne Blanche, Guerchère and others) may be sold as Morgeot. The name comes from the Abbaye de Morgeot, a farm of the Cistercian abbey of Maizières whose chapel still stands among the vines.

Morgeot white is the broadest and most generous of Chassagne: ripe citrus, hazelnut and a round, mouth-filling texture with a firm mineral spine. It is also one of the few Côte de Beaune premier crus with a serious red tradition: until the 1970s Chassagne was mostly a red-wine village, and Morgeot rouge is sturdy and dark-fruited.
appellations.terroir: East-southeast-facing at 225 to 265 m, gentle slope at the southern end of the commune toward Santenay. Brown limestone-clay, with more clay and marl than the northern premier crus, over Bathonian limestone.
appellations.nerd_note: Because so many lieux-dits can use the name, a Chassagne 'Morgeot' can come from very different sites: check the small print for the lieu-dit.

appellations.name: Chassagne-Montrachet premier cru Petingeret
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay (Pinot Blanc permitted); Pinot Noir for the rarer reds
appellations.summary: Petingeret is a 1.8 ha part of Les Vergers, at the Saint-Aubin boundary.
appellations.terroir: East-facing at 255 to 270 m, gentle slope, stony limestone-clay. On the map it lies above Saint-Aubin's Pitangeret and Les Pasquelles and beside Les Vergers and Saint-Aubin's Les Combes.
appellations.nerd_note: Saint-Aubin's Pitangeret is the same climat across the commune line.

appellations.name: Chassagne-Montrachet premier cru Tonton Marcel
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay (Pinot Blanc permitted); Pinot Noir for the rarer reds
appellations.summary: Tonton Marcel ('Uncle Marcel') is a tiny 0.50 ha premier cru within La Grande Montagne, on the steep upper slope. It is one of the most improbable names in the Burgundy classification.
appellations.terroir: Very steep, east-southeast-facing at 305 to 340 m, slope around 30%, thin stony soil. On the map it lies above La Grande Montagne.
appellations.nerd_note: The name presumably honours a former owner.

appellations.name: Chassagne-Montrachet premier cru Tête du Clos
match: Chassagne-Montrachet premier cru Tête du Clos
Chassagne-Montrachet Premier Cru Tête du Clos
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay (Pinot Blanc permitted); Pinot Noir for the rarer reds
appellations.summary: Tête du Clos is a 2.1 ha part of Morgeot, at the top of Les Grands Clos.
appellations.terroir: East-southeast-facing at 250 to 275 m, moderately steep, stony limestone soils. On the map it lies below Bois de Chassagne, above Les Grands Clos and Les Brussonnes and beside Francemont.
appellations.nerd_note: It may be sold under its own name or as Morgeot.

appellations.name: Chassagne-Montrachet premier cru Vide Bourse
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay (Pinot Blanc permitted); Pinot Noir for the rarer reds
appellations.summary: Vide Bourse ('empty purse') is a 1.3 ha premier cru just south of Bâtard-Montrachet and Criots-Bâtard-Montrachet. Fernand et Laurent Pillot make a well-known version. The wine is rich and mineral.
appellations.terroir: Almost flat, south exposure at about 240 m, brown limestone-clay.
appellations.nerd_note: The name may refer to the cost of farming it, or to the price paid for it.

appellations.name: Chassagne-Montrachet premier cru Vigne Blanche
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay (Pinot Blanc permitted); Pinot Noir for the rarer reds
appellations.summary: Vigne Blanche is a 2.2 ha part of Morgeot. The name suggests it was always a white-wine site.
appellations.terroir: Southeast-facing at 235 to 245 m, gentle slope, pale limestone-clay. On the map it lies below Les Petits Clos and beside Morgeot, La Boudriotte and Abbaye de Morgeot.
appellations.nerd_note: It may be sold under its own name or as Morgeot.

appellations.name: Chassagne-Montrachet premier cru Vigne Derrière
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay (Pinot Blanc permitted); Pinot Noir for the rarer reds
appellations.summary: Vigne Derrière is a 3.8 ha part of the Cailleret umbrella, just south of the village.
appellations.terroir: East-southeast-facing at 250 to 290 m, moderately steep, stony limestone soils. On the map it lies below Cailleret and En Cailleret and above Chassagne and Les Champs gain.
appellations.nerd_note: It may be sold under its own name or as Cailleret.

appellations.name: Corton Basses Mourottes
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: Les Basses Mourottes is a small 0.94 ha Corton climat on the northeast face of the hill, in Ladoix. The wine is firm and fresh.
appellations.terroir: East-southeast-facing at 285 to 305 m, moderately steep, brown limestone-clay with marl. On the map it lies below the grand cru Corton-Charlemagne and Corton Hautes Mourottes, above the grand cru Corton and beside Ladoix's Basses Mourottes.
appellations.nerd_note: The Ladoix premier cru of the same name lies beside it.

appellations.name: Corton Clos des Meix
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary:
The Clos des Meix is a walled 2.2 ha Corton climat on the southwest face of the hill, a monopole of Domaine Comte Senard, which makes red Corton here and some white.

The clos lies on the southwest side of the hill, beside Les Combes and La Vigne au Saint and just above Aloxe's Clos du Chapitre. Senard, based in Aloxe, has owned it for generations and makes a supple, red-fruited Corton from it, as well as one of the rare white Cortons.
appellations.terroir: Southwest-facing at 240 to 260 m, gentle slope, brown limestone-clay. The southwest exposure, unusual on the Côte, gives the clos warm afternoons and a ripe, round style.
appellations.nerd_note: Senard is one of the few estates to make a white wine labelled Corton rather than Corton-Charlemagne.

appellations.name: Corton Hautes Mourottes
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: Les Hautes Mourottes is a 1.9 ha Corton climat high on the northeast face of the hill, in Ladoix. The wine is lean and fresh.
appellations.terroir: Steep, east-southeast-facing at 300 to 330 m, slope around 18%, thin marly limestone soils. On the map it lies below Ladoix's Hautes Mourottes and above the grand cru Corton-Charlemagne, Corton Le Rognet et Corton and Corton Basses Mourottes.
appellations.nerd_note: The Ladoix premier cru of the same name lies beside it.

appellations.name: Corton La Toppe au Vert
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: La Toppe au Vert is a tiny 0.11 ha Corton climat on the lower east face of the hill, above the Aloxe-Corton premier cru of the same name.
appellations.terroir: East-southeast-facing at 230 to 240 m, moderately steep, brown limestone-clay.
appellations.nerd_note: At barely an eighth of a hectare it is the smallest Corton climat on the map; the Aloxe-Corton premier cru La Toppe au Vert lies just below.

appellations.name: Corton La Vigne au Saint
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: La Vigne au Saint is a 2.5 ha Corton climat on the southwest face of the hill. Louis Latour bottles its walled heart as Corton Clos de la Vigne au Saint, a monopole. The wine is firm and red-fruited.
appellations.terroir: South-southwest-facing at 245 to 260 m, gentle slope, brown limestone-clay.
appellations.nerd_note: Latour's Château Corton Grancey, the estate's other Corton, is a blend of several climats, while the Clos de la Vigne au Saint is a single site.

appellations.name: Corton Le Clos du Roi
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary:
Le Clos du Roi is the climat most often named the finest red of Corton. It lies mid-slope on the southeast face of the hill, at 10.9 ha, and takes its name from the Dukes of Burgundy, whose vineyard it was before passing to the French crown in 1477.

Its wines combine Corton's structure with unusual finesse: dark cherry, spice and a firm but fine tannin that needs ten years. Comte Senard, Follin-Arbelet, de Montille and the Prince de Mérode (whose holding has been leased to the Domaine de la Romanée-Conti since 2009) are leading holders.
appellations.terroir: Southeast-facing at 275 to 325 m, moderately steep. Brown limestone-clay with iron, over Bathonian limestone, below the band of marl that carries Corton-Charlemagne.
appellations.nerd_note: The DRC's Corton is a blend of Clos du Roi, Bressandes and Renardes from the Mérode lease.

appellations.name: Corton Le Corton
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary:
Le Corton is the climat at the top of the hill's southeast face, at 11.7 ha, just below the woods that crown the hill. It gives some of the most structured red Cortons.

Le Corton occupies the upper part of the southeast face, just below the Bois de Corton, with Les Renardes and Le Clos du Roi below it and Corton-Charlemagne's white-wine marls alongside. Its steep, thin soils give a firm, sometimes austere red that can be one of the longest-lived Cortons; Bouchard Père et Fils' 'Le Corton' is the most widely seen.
appellations.terroir: Steep, southeast-facing at 310 to 365 m, slope around 24%. Thin marl and limestone soils.
appellations.nerd_note: Le Corton sits right under the Bois de Corton, the cap of woodland that keeps the hilltop cool and feeds it cold air at night.

appellations.name: Corton Le Meix Lallemand
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: Le Meix Lallemand is a small 0.55 ha Corton climat on the southwest face of the hill. The wine is usually blended with other Corton climats.
appellations.terroir: South-southwest-facing at 250 to 265 m, gentle slope, brown limestone-clay.
appellations.nerd_note: A *meix* is a plot attached to a house: this was once a garden-vineyard on the edge of Aloxe.

appellations.name: Corton Le Rognet et Corton
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary:
Le Rognet et Corton is a 11.8 ha Corton climat on the hill's east face, in Ladoix-Serrigny. Faiveley's monopole Clos des Cortons Faiveley is inside it, and Méo-Camuzet makes a Corton Clos Rognet.

Le Rognet et Corton is the largest Corton climat on the Ladoix side of the hill, on the east face below the Ladoix premier cru of the same name and beside Les Renardes. Faiveley's walled Clos des Cortons Faiveley, about 3 ha, is the most famous wine from it: dense, spicy and long-lived.
appellations.terroir: East-southeast-facing at 245 to 320 m, moderately steep, brown limestone-clay with marl.
appellations.nerd_note: The Clos des Cortons Faiveley is the only climat in Burgundy allowed to carry its owner's name as part of the vineyard name.

appellations.name: Corton Les Bressandes
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary:
Les Bressandes is the largest red climat of Corton, at 17.2 ha, on the lower and middle slope of the hill's southeast face. It is often ranked with Clos du Roi as the finest: its wines are generous, red-fruited and perfumed, with a softer, more approachable tannin than Clos du Roi.

Its position below Le Clos du Roi and Les Renardes and above Aloxe's Les Valozières explains its generosity: where Clos du Roi is firm and Renardes wild, Bressandes is the most immediately charming red Corton, though the best bottles still age for twenty years. Tollot-Beaut and Chandon de Briailles make classic, perfumed versions.
appellations.terroir: Southeast-facing at 250 to 275 m, gentle slope, deeper brown limestone-clay with some red iron-rich soil.
appellations.nerd_note: The Hospices de Beaune's Corton cuvées Charlotte Dumay and Docteur Peste both draw on Bressandes vines.

appellations.name: Corton Les Carrières
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: Les Carrières is a small 0.48 ha Corton climat on the east face of the hill, in Ladoix. The name refers to old quarries.
appellations.terroir: East-southeast-facing at 270 to 295 m, moderately steep, stony limestone soils. On the map it lies below the grand cru Corton-Charlemagne, above Ladoix's Bois Roussot and beside the grand cru Corton and Corton Le Rognet et Corton.
appellations.nerd_note: Its neighbours Le Rognet and Les Moutottes complete the Ladoix side of the grand cru.

appellations.name: Corton Les Chaumes
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: Les Chaumes (officially Les Chaumes et la Voierosse) is a 6.7 ha Corton climat on the southwest face of the hill, toward Pernand. The wine is supple and red-fruited.
appellations.terroir: Southwest-facing at 245 to 270 m, gentle slope, brown limestone-clay. On the map it lies below the grand cru Charlemagne, the grand cru Corton-Charlemagne and Corton Les Pougets and above Corton La Vigne au Saint.
appellations.nerd_note: *Chaumes* means fallow or stubble land.

appellations.name: Corton Les Combes
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: Les Combes is a 1.7 ha Corton climat at the southwest foot of the hill. The wine is supple and fruity.
appellations.terroir: South-southwest-facing at 240 to 255 m, gentle slope, brown limestone-clay. On the map it lies below Corton La Vigne au Saint and beside Corton Clos des Meix.
appellations.nerd_note: *Combes* refers to small valleys in the hill.

appellations.name: Corton Les Fiètres
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: Les Fiètres is a small 1.1 ha Corton climat on the southwest face of the hill. The wine is supple and red-fruited.
appellations.terroir: South-facing at about 260 m, gentle slope, brown limestone-clay. On the map it lies below Corton Les Perrières, above Corton Clos des Meix and beside Corton Les Chaumes and Corton Le Meix Lallemand.
appellations.nerd_note: The Hospices de Beaune's Corton cuvée Docteur Peste includes vines here.

appellations.name: Corton Les Grandes Lolières
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: Les Grandes Lolières is a 3.0 ha Corton climat on the lower east face of the hill, in Ladoix. The wine is supple for a Corton.
appellations.terroir: East-southeast-facing at 240 to 265 m, gentle slope, brown limestone-clay. On the map it lies below Corton Le Rognet et Corton and Corton Les Moutottes, above Aloxe-Corton's La Coutière and beside Aloxe-Corton's Les Petites Folières.
appellations.nerd_note: Its lower edge meets the Aloxe-Corton premier crus La Coutière and Les Petites Folières.

appellations.name: Corton Les Grèves
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary:
Les Grèves is a 2.3 ha Corton climat on the southern slope of the hill, near Les Perrières. *Grèves* means gravel. The wine is fine and red-fruited.

Les Grèves is a small climat on the southern face, between Les Perrières and Les Bressandes, on gravelly limestone (*grèves*). It makes one of the finer, more perfumed red Cortons, and the Hospices de Beaune's cuvée Docteur Peste blends it with Bressandes, Chaumes, Fiètres and Clos du Roi.
appellations.terroir: Southeast-facing at 260 to 275 m, gentle slope, gravelly limestone soils.
appellations.nerd_note: The Hospices de Beaune's Corton cuvée Docteur Peste includes vines in Les Grèves.

appellations.name: Corton Les Languettes
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary:
Les Languettes is a 7.2 ha Corton climat on the south face of the hill, below Corton-Charlemagne. Most of it is planted with Chardonnay and sold as Corton-Charlemagne; the red is rare.

It sits on the steep south face below the Bois de Corton, between Le Corton and Les Pougets, on thin white marl, the soil that gives Corton-Charlemagne its tension. Its narrow strips are planted mostly to Chardonnay, which is why a red Corton Languettes is one of the rarest names in the grand cru.
appellations.terroir: Steep, south-southeast-facing at 285 to 355 m, slope around 21%. Thin white marl soils. At 285 to 355 m and with a median gradient near 21%, it is one of the steepest climats on the hill.
appellations.nerd_note: The name describes the narrow, tongue-like strips the parcels form on the slope.

appellations.name: Corton Les Maréchaudes
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary:
Les Maréchaudes is a 4.4 ha Corton climat on the lower east face of the hill, toward Ladoix. The wine is supple and fruity for a Corton.

It is the point where the grand cru gives way to the Aloxe-Corton premiers crus of the same name, with Les Bressandes and Les Vergennes above. Its deeper soils give a softer, rounder Corton that drinks earlier than the climats higher up.
appellations.terroir: Southeast-facing at 230 to 250 m, gentle slope, brown limestone-clay. The gradient is moderate, about 13%, and the deeper soil at the foot of the hill holds more water than the stony upper climats.
appellations.nerd_note: Mérode kept its Maréchaudes when it leased its other Corton vines to the Domaine de la Romanée-Conti in 2009.

appellations.name: Corton Les Moutottes
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: Les Moutottes is a small 0.81 ha Corton climat on the east face of the hill, in Ladoix, beside the Aloxe-Corton premier cru of the same name.
appellations.terroir: East-southeast-facing at 250 to 270 m, moderately steep, brown limestone-clay. On the map it lies below Corton Le Rognet et Corton, above Corton Les Grandes Lolières and Aloxe-Corton's Les Petites Folières and beside Aloxe-Corton's Les Moutottes.
appellations.nerd_note: Part of the lieu-dit is grand cru and part premier cru.

appellations.name: Corton Les Paulands
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: Les Paulands is a small 1.1 ha Corton climat above the Aloxe-Corton premier cru of the same name, on the lower slope of the hill.
appellations.terroir: East-southeast-facing at 240 to 255 m, moderately steep, brown limestone-clay. On the map it lies below the grand cru Corton and Corton Les Bressandes, above Aloxe-Corton's Les Paulands and beside Aloxe-Corton's Les Valozières.
appellations.nerd_note: Its lower section is classed only as Aloxe-Corton premier cru.

appellations.name: Corton Les Perrières
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary:
Les Perrières is a 10.0 ha Corton climat on the southern slope of the hill, below Les Pougets. The name refers to old quarries. The wine is firm and mineral.

With Les Pougets and Les Languettes above and Les Grèves alongside, it makes a firm, mineral red, more linear than Bressandes, and Méo-Camuzet's version has helped make the name better known.
appellations.terroir: South-southeast-facing at 260 to 290 m, gentle slope, stony limestone soils. Old quarry workings and limestone rubble give it some of the stoniest soil among the red Corton climats.
appellations.nerd_note: Its lower edge touches Aloxe-Corton's premier crus Les Fournières and Les Chaillots.

appellations.name: Corton Les Pougets
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary:
Les Pougets is a 9.8 ha Corton climat on the southwest face of the hill, below Corton-Charlemagne. Louis Jadot's Corton Pougets is the reference: a fine, perfumed red.

Les Pougets lies on the southwest side of the hill, toward Pernand, below Les Languettes and above Les Chaumes, on marly limestone that is equally good for Chardonnay. Jadot farms both colours here: the red Corton Pougets is perfumed and fine, and Chardonnay from the upper part goes into its Corton-Charlemagne.
appellations.terroir: South-southwest-facing at 270 to 325 m, moderately steep, marly limestone soils. The southwest-facing side of the hill warms in the afternoon, which helps both Pinot Noir and Chardonnay ripen fully on this marly soil.
appellations.nerd_note: The upper part of Les Pougets is planted with Chardonnay and sold as Corton-Charlemagne.

appellations.name: Corton Les Renardes
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary:
Les Renardes ('the foxes') is a large 14.3 ha Corton climat on the upper part of the hill's east face, toward Ladoix. Its wines are the most gamey and wild of Corton, with dark fruit, earth and a firm tannin.

Its neighbours are Le Corton above, Le Clos du Roi to the southwest and Le Rognet toward Ladoix, and the iron-rich soil with marl is what gives the wine its earthy depth. The Prince de Mérode vines leased to the Domaine de la Romanée-Conti since 2009 form part of the DRC's Corton.
appellations.terroir: Southeast-facing at 275 to 335 m, moderately steep, iron-rich brown limestone-clay.
appellations.nerd_note: Tasters often say the name fits the wine: Renardes has a feral, foxy note.

appellations.name: Corton Les Vergennes
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary:
Les Vergennes is a 3.5 ha Corton climat on the east face of the hill, toward Ladoix. The Hospices de Beaune's Corton Vergennes cuvée Paul Chanson is a white Corton.

It sits below Le Rognet and above the Aloxe premier cru La Toppe au Vert. The Hospices de Beaune's cuvée Paul Chanson, from this climat, is a white Corton, which shows that the hill's whites are not confined to Corton-Charlemagne.
appellations.terroir: Southeast-facing at 235 to 270 m, moderately steep, brown limestone-clay with marl. The marl here, close to that of Corton-Charlemagne, is why the Hospices chose to plant Chardonnay.
appellations.nerd_note: The Hospices' cuvée Paul Chanson is one of the few white wines sold under the Corton name rather than Corton-Charlemagne.

appellations.name: Fixin premier cru Arvelets
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir; Chardonnay and Pinot Blanc for the rare whites
appellations.summary: A small upper-slope premier cru of 3.3 ha next to Les Hervelets, at the northern end of Fixin. Because the appellation rules allow its wine to be sold as Les Hervelets, the name Arvelets rarely appears on a label. The style is the same: firm, red-fruited Fixin with a mineral grip.
appellations.terroir: East-southeast exposure at 315 to 345 m, on thin limestone and stony scree.
appellations.nerd_note: Arvelets and Hervelets sit side by side at almost the same altitude, and many growers treat them as one vineyard.

appellations.name: Fixin premier cru Clos Napoléon
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir; Chardonnay and Pinot Blanc for the rare whites
appellations.summary:
Fixin's Clos Napoléon is a shrine as much as a vineyard. Claude Noisot, a captain of Napoleon's Imperial Guard who followed the emperor to Elba, retired to Fixin, renamed his walled vineyard (formerly Aux Cheusots) in his honour and in 1847 commissioned François Rude's bronze 'Napoleon Awakening to Immortality', which still stands in the Parc Noisot above the vines. The clos is today a monopole of Domaine Pierre Gelin, at 1.8 ha.

The wine is a little rounder and earlier than the Clos de la Perrière next door, with red and black fruit, a savoury, earthy edge and Fixin's characteristic firm finish. It is one of the few places on the Côte de Nuits where a premier cru from a serious estate still sells at a village-wine price.
appellations.terroir: Mid-slope, east-southeast exposure at 310 to 325 m, just below the Clos de la Perrière. Brown limestone soils with more clay than the clos above, over Bajocian marl and limestone.
appellations.nerd_note: Noisot asked to be buried standing up, facing his emperor's statue; his tomb is in the park beside the vines.

appellations.name: Fixin premier cru Clos de la Perrière
match: Fixin premier cru Clos de la Perrière
Fixin 1er Cru Clos de la Perrière
Fixin Premier Cru Clos de la Perrière
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir; Chardonnay and Pinot Blanc for the rare whites
appellations.summary:
The Clos de la Perrière is the grandest wine of Fixin and, by old reputation, one of the best sites of the whole northern Côte. It sits above the hamlet behind the walls of the Manoir de la Perrière, which monks of Cîteaux built around 1142 with stone from a quarry just up the hill (the *perrière* of the name). The monks farmed it until 1622, and the boundaries are thought to be unchanged since they planted it. In the 19th century it was ranked a *tête de cuvée*, the only one outside Chambertin and Clos de Bèze in this part of the Côte, and it sold at the same price.

The Joliet family has owned it since 1853, and Bénigne Joliet, the sixth generation, bought out his relatives in 2004 to make it a true monopole. The INAO delimitation measures 5.9 ha, of which about 4 ha are planted, and a corner reaches into Brochon. The wine is darker and more rustic than Gevrey's grands crus, with black cherry, iron and a firm, slightly wild tannin that needs eight to ten years; since 2005, with lower yields and more care, it has been chasing its old reputation.
appellations.terroir: Steep, east-southeast-facing slope at 320 to 360 m, among the highest premier crus in Fixin. Thin brown limestone soils over Bajocian and Bathonian rock with very little clay. A breeze from the Combe de Fixin cools the upper vines, which ripen several days after the lower ones.
appellations.nerd_note: The 12th-century vaulted cuverie still holds the monks' original beam press, last used in 1959.

appellations.name: Fixin premier cru Clos du Chapitre
match: Fixin premier cru Clos du Chapitre
Fixin Premier Cru Clos du Chapitre
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir; Chardonnay and Pinot Blanc for the rare whites
appellations.summary: A walled clos that once belonged to a cathedral chapter, hence its name, and one of Fixin's six premier crus. At 4.8 ha it lies just below and beside the Clos de la Perrière and the Clos Napoléon, on the gentler part of the slope; an 1855 description said its wine resembled La Perrière's and that only a wall separated them. Its wines are sturdy and dark-fruited, with Fixin's slightly rustic tannin but more flesh than the steeper climats above.
appellations.terroir: East-facing at 305 to 330 m. Brown calcareous clay over limestone, deeper than the soils of the Clos de la Perrière.
appellations.nerd_note: Gevrey-Chambertin also has a premier cru called Clos du Chapitre: both recall the ecclesiastical chapters that owned so much of the Côte before 1789.

appellations.name: Fixin premier cru Hervelets
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir; Chardonnay and Pinot Blanc for the rare whites
appellations.summary:
Les Hervelets is the most widely seen Fixin premier cru, partly because the neighbouring Arvelets may be sold under its name. It occupies 3.7 ha of the upper slope at the northern end of the commune, toward Brochon, and gives a slightly finer, more perfumed Fixin than the Clos du Chapitre, with red cherry, spice and a mineral, stony finish.

Les Hervelets lies on the upper slope just south of Brochon, above Les Meix Bas and next to Les Arvelets, and its altitude and thin soil make it the most aromatic of Fixin's premier crus. It is often the best entry to the village's style: firm, red-fruited and long-lived, a cheaper and wilder cousin of the Côte de Nuits' more famous names.
appellations.terroir: Southeast-facing at 310 to 350 m. Thin, stony limestone soils with a little marl, cooled by air from the Combe de Fixin.
appellations.nerd_note: Fixin's rules let Les Arvelets be labelled Les Hervelets, which is why the larger name is the one you see in shops.

appellations.name: Fixin premier cru Les Meix Bas
match: Fixin premier cru Les Meix Bas
Fixin Premier Cru Les Meix Bas
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir; Chardonnay and Pinot Blanc for the rare whites
appellations.summary: The smallest of Fixin's premier crus at only 0.49 ha, a sliver below Les Hervelets. A *meix* in Burgundian dialect is a plot attached to a house, so this was once a garden-vineyard on the edge of the hamlet. Little is bottled separately; most goes into Fixin premier cru blends.
appellations.terroir: East-southeast-facing at 310 to 320 m, on brown limestone soils with some clay washed down from Les Hervelets.
appellations.nerd_note: Fixin also permits white wine from its premier crus, though almost none is made.

appellations.name: Gevrey-Chambertin premier cru Au Closeau
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: Au Closeau ('the little enclosure') is a tiny premier cru of 0.53 ha just north of Mazis-Chambertin, at the edge of the village. The wine is a soft, early-drinking Gevrey premier cru.
appellations.terroir: Flat, southeast exposure at about 275 m, on deep brown limestone-clay. On the map it lies below the grand cru Mazis-Chambertin and beside La Perrière and Les Corbeaux.
appellations.nerd_note: It is one of the smallest premier crus in Gevrey.

appellations.name: Gevrey-Chambertin premier cru Aux Combottes
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary:
Aux Combottes is the premier cru islanded among grands crus: Latricières-Chambertin to the north, Mazoyères and Charmes-Chambertin to the east and Clos de la Roche to the south. At 4.6 ha it sits in a slight hollow, which is the usual explanation for its exclusion from grand cru (cold air pools here and the soils are a little deeper). In practice its wines are among the most refined premier crus in Gevrey, with the perfume and silk of the Morey grands crus next door.

Dujac is a major holder, and its Combottes is consistently one of the domaine's best wines below grand cru level.
appellations.terroir: East-southeast-facing at 270 to 285 m, in a shallow depression. Brown limestone-clay with Bajocian marl at depth.
appellations.nerd_note: Aux Combottes is often cited as the clearest case in Burgundy where the soil looks like grand cru but a local cold pocket kept it out.

appellations.name: Gevrey-Chambertin premier cru Bel Air
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary:
Bel Air is the premier cru directly above Chambertin and Clos de Bèze, at 2.6 ha, where the slope steepens toward the woods. The wine is lean, fresh and stony, much lighter than the grands crus below, because the soils are thinner and the site cooler.

Ruchottes and Mazis lie to the north, and the vines give way to scrub and woodland just above. In cooler decades it struggled to ripen; in recent hot summers its freshness has become an advantage, and growers increasingly value it as a source of lift for their premier cru blends.
appellations.terroir: Steep, east-facing at 300 to 330 m, slope near 23%. Thin soil over hard limestone at the top of the Chambertin slope.
appellations.nerd_note: Bel Air shows how fast terroir changes in Burgundy: a few metres upslope from Chambertin, the soil thins and the wine drops a full rank.

appellations.name: Gevrey-Chambertin premier cru Champeaux
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary:
Champeaux lies at the northern end of the Côte Saint-Jacques, toward Brochon, on a slope of stony, thin soils. At 6.7 ha it is a mid-sized premier cru that makes a lighter, more aromatic Gevrey than Les Cazetiers: red cherry, wild strawberry and a stony, mineral bite, ready earlier.

In the hands of Denis Mortet and Fourrier it has a cult following as one of Gevrey's most transparent premier crus.

Champeaux marks the point where the Côte Saint-Jacques runs out toward Brochon, so it sits below the steep, high Goulots and Combe au Moine and beside the Petits Cazetiers. It is a good example of how Gevrey's northern premier crus differ from the grands crus south of the village: less flesh and power, more transparency and lift, and a stony finish that reflects the shallow soil.
appellations.terroir: East-southeast-facing at 315 to 350 m, on thin, rocky limestone with little topsoil, below Les Goulots and Combe au Moine.
appellations.nerd_note: Champeaux is one of the stoniest vineyards in Gevrey: the topsoil is so thin that the vines root almost directly into fissured limestone.

appellations.name: Gevrey-Chambertin premier cru Champonnet
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: A 3.3 ha premier cru on the flat ground just north of Ruchottes-Chambertin, between the village and the grands crus. The wine is a medium-bodied, red-fruited Gevrey premier cru.
appellations.terroir: Gentle northeast exposure at 285 to 295 m, on brown limestone-clay with alluvial gravel.
appellations.nerd_note: Champonnet, Craipillot and Fonteny together sit where the Lavaux stream's alluvial fan meets the slope, so their soils are deeper and more gravelly than the grands crus just south.

appellations.name: Gevrey-Chambertin premier cru Cherbaudes
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary:
Cherbaudes sits at 2.2 ha between Mazis-Chambertin and Chapelle-Chambertin, almost surrounded by grands crus. Fourrier's 'Vieilles Vignes' bottling shows the site's best: a silky, perfumed wine with a grand cru's finesse in a lighter frame. The soil is close to that of the neighbouring grands crus, and some growers argue it deserved promotion.

Cherbaudes is effectively a premier cru island inside the grand cru zone: Mazis-Chambertin lies to the west, Chapelle-Chambertin to the south and Chambertin-Clos de Bèze just beyond. It is a vivid example of the INAO's 1930s approach in Gevrey, which classified by reputation and tradition rather than by drawing smooth lines across the slope.
appellations.terroir: East-southeast-facing at 265 to 275 m, almost flat, on brown limestone-clay over Bathonian rock.
appellations.nerd_note: It is one of Gevrey's few premier crus that touches four grands crus.

appellations.name: Gevrey-Chambertin premier cru Clos Prieur
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: Only the upper part of the Clos Prieur is premier cru: at 2.0 ha it lies just east of Mazis-Chambertin, while the lower half is village Gevrey. The wine is a fleshy, red-fruited premier cru, softer than Mazis.
appellations.terroir: East-southeast-facing at about 270 m, on deep brown limestone-clay.
appellations.nerd_note: The name points to a prior, a sign that the land belonged to a religious house before the Revolution.

appellations.name: Gevrey-Chambertin premier cru Clos Saint-Jacques
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary:
Clos Saint-Jacques is the premier cru everyone agrees should be a grand cru; it sells for more than most of Gevrey's grands crus. It lies on the Côte Saint-Jacques, the slope that bends round to face southeast just north of the village. In the 1930s the new INAO granted grand cru status in Gevrey only to vineyards adjoining Chambertin or Clos de Bèze; this one is detached on the far side of the village, so it was classed premier cru, even though Lavalle (1855) and Rodier (1920) had put it in the top rank.

The Comte de Moucheron held it as a monopole through the 19th century and sold it in 1954. Today its 6.7 ha (the INAO delimitation gives 6.7 ha) are split between five owners, each with a strip running from top to bottom of the slope: Armand Rousseau (2.2 ha), Sylvie Esmonin (1.6 ha), Bruno Clair and Louis Jadot (1 ha each, from the old Clair-Daü holding) and Fourrier (0.89 ha). Every owner has the same cross-section of soils, so it is a perfect test of winemaking.

The wine joins Gevrey's power to unusual elegance: dense red and black fruit, fine tannin and a cool, mineral finish, built for 20 years or more.
appellations.terroir: Southeast-facing at 290 to 350 m, with a moderate slope. Thin, stony soil on hard Bathonian limestone at the top; deeper brown limestone-clay washed from the Combe de Lavaux lower down. Cold air draining from the combe slows ripening and keeps acidity.
appellations.nerd_note: Until the 1954 sale the bottom of the clos grew alfalfa. Rousseau prices its Clos Saint-Jacques above its Mazis, Ruchottes and Charmes-Chambertin.

appellations.name: Gevrey-Chambertin premier cru Clos des Varoilles
match: Gevrey-Chambertin premier cru Clos des Varoilles
Gevrey-Chambertin Premier Cru Clos des Varoilles
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary:
The Clos des Varoilles is a walled vineyard of 6.0 ha high in the Combe de Lavaux, on its southern flank, facing across the valley toward the Côte Saint-Jacques. It was for decades the flagship monopole of Domaine des Varoilles, and after that estate's division in 2020 the wine has been made by Prieuré-Roch (from the 2021 vintage).

Its wines are sturdy and long-lived, deep in colour, with dark cherry, spice and a firm, slightly wild tannin.
appellations.terroir: Steep, southeast-facing at 310 to 340 m, unusually for a Gevrey premier cru that sits inside the combe rather than on the main slope. Limestone scree and thin brown soils.
appellations.nerd_note: The clos is one of the few Gevrey premier crus that faces south-southeast across the Combe de Lavaux rather than east onto the plain.

appellations.name: Gevrey-Chambertin premier cru Clos du Chapitre
match: Gevrey-Chambertin premier cru Clos du Chapitre
Gevrey-Chambertin Premier Cru Clos du Chapitre
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: A small walled clos of 0.98 ha just below Clos Saint-Jacques, on the edge of the village. The chapter in its name was the cathedral chapter that owned vines here before the Revolution. The wine is a supple, fruity Gevrey premier cru.
appellations.terroir: South-southeast-facing at 285 to 300 m, on deeper brown limestone-clay at the foot of the Côte Saint-Jacques.
appellations.nerd_note: Fixin, the next village north, has a premier cru with the same name.

appellations.name: Gevrey-Chambertin premier cru Combe au Moine
match: Gevrey-Chambertin premier cru Combe au Moine
Gevrey-Chambertin Premier Cru Combe au Moine
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary:
Combe au Moine, the 'monk's valley', climbs steeply up the side of the Combe de Lavaux above Les Cazetiers. The monks are usually said to be those of Cluny, whose abbey was the dominant landowner in Gevrey in the Middle Ages. At 4.8 ha it is one of the highest premier crus in Gevrey, and the altitude shows: the wines are firm, lean and stony in youth, with sour cherry, herbs and a fresh, persistent finish, and they used to struggle in cool years.

Warmer vintages since 2000 have flattered the site, and in a hot year a Combe au Moine can outshine the lower climats, holding acidity that they lose.
appellations.terroir: Very steep, east-facing slope at 325 to 385 m. Thin, stony soil over hard limestone, with scree from the combe's walls. Exposed to cold air from the valley.
appellations.nerd_note: Fourrier's Combe au Moine is a Vieilles Vignes cuvée and one of the estate's most sought-after premier crus.

appellations.name: Gevrey-Chambertin premier cru Craipillot
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: A 2.8 ha premier cru on the gentle lower slope between the village and the grands crus, just south of the Clos du Chapitre. It gives a soft, fruity, early-drinking Gevrey premier cru.
appellations.terroir: Almost flat, east-southeast exposure at about 285 m, on deep brown limestone-clay and alluvial gravel from the Combe de Lavaux.
appellations.nerd_note: Its neighbours Champonnet and Fonteny form a small cluster of premier crus on the village side of Ruchottes-Chambertin.

appellations.name: Gevrey-Chambertin premier cru En Ergot
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: A small premier cru of 1.2 ha below Petite Chapelle, at the bottom of the slope near the Route des Grands Crus. The wine is a soft, fruity Gevrey premier cru.
appellations.terroir: Flat, southeast-facing at 255 to 265 m, on deep brown clay soils. On the map it lies beside Petite Chapelle.
appellations.nerd_note: An *ergot* is a spur, probably the shape of the parcel.

appellations.name: Gevrey-Chambertin premier cru Estournelles-Saint-Jacques
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary:
Estournelles-Saint-Jacques sits above Lavaut Saint-Jacques and west of Clos Saint-Jacques, curling into the Combe de Lavaux. At 2.0 ha it is a small, high site, and its wines are among the most refined of the Côte Saint-Jacques: perfumed, red-fruited and silky, less dense than Clos Saint-Jacques but with a similar cool, mineral finish.

Its position in the combe makes it a late ripener, and it rewards a grower who waits.

In the hierarchy of the Côte Saint-Jacques it is usually placed just behind Clos Saint-Jacques, Lavaut and Les Cazetiers, but in warm vintages its altitude and thin soil give it the freshest balance of the four. Humbert Frères' version is a byword for perfume, and Frédéric Esmonin's shows the firmer, stonier side of the site.
appellations.terroir: South-southeast-facing at 315 to 355 m on a steep slope. Very thin, stony soil over limestone.
appellations.nerd_note: Unlike its neighbours on the Côte Saint-Jacques, Estournelles turns to face south-southeast as the slope bends into the combe, so it catches more afternoon sun than Lavaut below.

appellations.name: Gevrey-Chambertin premier cru Fonteny
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary:
Fonteny sits just above Ruchottes-Chambertin and Mazis-Chambertin, at 3.7 ha, and gives one of the more elegant premier crus from the village side of the grands crus: red fruit, a silky texture and a stony finish. Joseph Roty's version is a benchmark.

Fonteny belongs to the small group of premier crus on the northern edge of the grand cru zone, between the village and Ruchottes-Chambertin, with Champonnet and Craipillot just below. Its upper edge rises onto thinner, stonier ground, which is why the best Fontenys have more tension than the neighbouring lower-slope premier crus.
appellations.terroir: East-northeast-facing at 280 to 300 m, on thin brown limestone over Bathonian rock, rising toward the woods.
appellations.nerd_note: Fonteny is one of the few premier crus that sits above two grands crus at once, with Ruchottes and Mazis-Chambertin along its lower edge.

appellations.name: Gevrey-Chambertin premier cru Issarts
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: A tiny premier cru of 0.62 ha above Fonteny and next to Ruchottes-Chambertin. *Issarts* means land cleared from the forest. Faiveley is the main producer and the wine is firm and fresh, with a grand cru neighbour's structure in a lighter frame.
appellations.terroir: East-northeast-facing at 300 to 315 m, on thin stony limestone soils.
appellations.nerd_note: Its grand cru neighbour Ruchottes-Chambertin shares the same thin soils over Bathonian rock.

appellations.name: Gevrey-Chambertin premier cru La Bossière
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: La Bossière is a tiny premier cru of 0.45 ha in the Combe de Lavaux, next to the Clos des Varoilles. It is a monopole of Domaine Harmand-Geoffroy, which makes a firm, fresh wine with red fruit, herbs and a lean, stony finish typical of the combe's high sites.
appellations.terroir: East-facing at 325 to 335 m, on steep, thin limestone soils.
appellations.nerd_note: With the Clos des Varoilles and La Romanée, La Bossière is one of three premier crus tucked inside the Combe de Lavaux rather than on the main slope.

appellations.name: Gevrey-Chambertin premier cru La Perrière
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: A small premier cru of 2.5 ha in the lower part of the slope east of Mazis-Chambertin, near the village. The name, as so often in Burgundy, records an old stone quarry. The wine is a supple, fruity Gevrey premier cru.
appellations.terroir: Flat, southeast exposure at about 270 m, on brown limestone-clay.
appellations.nerd_note: Gevrey's quarries supplied stone for the village houses and for Dijon's buildings.

appellations.name: Gevrey-Chambertin premier cru La Romanée
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: Gevrey's La Romanée (not to be confused with the Vosne grand cru) is a steep 1.1 ha premier cru above the Clos des Varoilles, inside the Combe de Lavaux. It was long a monopole of Domaine des Varoilles, whose holdings were divided in 2020. The wine is lean, fresh and stony, a high-altitude Gevrey.
appellations.terroir: Very steep, south-southeast-facing at 335 to 360 m, with a median slope near 31%. Thin soil and scree over limestone.
appellations.nerd_note: There are three Romanées in Burgundy's premier and grand cru lists: the Vosne grand cru, this Gevrey premier cru and a Chassagne-Montrachet premier cru.

appellations.name: Gevrey-Chambertin premier cru Lavaut Saint-Jacques
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary:
Lavaut Saint-Jacques (often spelt Lavaux) sits just below and south of Clos Saint-Jacques, at the mouth of the Combe de Lavaux, the deep valley that cuts the hill behind Gevrey. At 9.6 ha it is one of the larger premier crus of the Côte Saint-Jacques, and in good hands it is the closest thing to Clos Saint-Jacques: perfumed, cherry-fruited and lifted, with a cooler, more floral profile than the grands crus south of the village and a long, slightly stony finish.

The cold air that slides out of the combe makes it a later-ripening site, which was a handicap in the 20th century and has become an asset with warmer summers.
appellations.terroir: Southeast-facing at 290 to 320 m, on a gentle slope. Brown limestone soils mixed with scree and gravel brought down by the Lavaux stream, with less clay than the Côte Saint-Jacques' upper climats.
appellations.nerd_note: Its name means 'the valley of Saint James': the combe and the Côte Saint-Jacques both take their name from a statue of Saint James on the pilgrim road to Compostela.

appellations.name: Gevrey-Chambertin premier cru Les Cazetiers
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary:
Les Cazetiers lies directly north of and above Clos Saint-Jacques on the Côte Saint-Jacques and is usually ranked third among the climats of that slope, after Clos Saint-Jacques and Lavaut. At 9.1 ha it has enough growers to show its character clearly: a deep, structured Gevrey, more muscular and darker-fruited than Clos Saint-Jacques, with a firmer tannin that needs a decade to settle.

The upper part is steep and thin-soiled, the lower part broader and gentler, so producers with vines in both often get the most complete wine.
appellations.terroir: Southeast exposure at 300 to 365 m. Brown limestone over hard Bathonian rock in the upper part, deeper limestone-clay lower down. The slope steepens sharply toward the woods.
appellations.nerd_note: Faiveley's holding grew when it bought Domaine Dupont-Tisserandot, one of the main Cazetiers growers, in 2013.

appellations.name: Gevrey-Chambertin premier cru Les Corbeaux
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary:
Les Corbeaux ('the crows') is a 3.2 ha premier cru just north of Mazis-Chambertin; the lower part of the lieu-dit is only village Gevrey. The wine is supple and perfumed, with dark cherry and a softer texture than the grand cru next door. Denis Bachelet's tiny old-vine bottling is one of the most coveted Gevrey premier crus.

Its position just north of Mazis-Chambertin, on the flat ground between the village and the grands crus, explains its style: deep soil gives roundness and early charm, while the Mazis influence brings a dark, spicy core. Lucien Boillot's version shows the more structured side of the site.
appellations.terroir: East-facing at 275 to 285 m, almost flat, on brown limestone-clay.
appellations.nerd_note: Bachelet makes only a few barrels from very old vines here, and the wine is allocated within days of release.

appellations.name: Gevrey-Chambertin premier cru Les Goulots
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: A steep premier cru of 1.8 ha at the top of the slope above Champeaux, at the northern end of the Côte Saint-Jacques. The wine is fresh and lean, with red fruit and a sharp, stony edge.
appellations.terroir: East-southeast-facing at 335 to 380 m, one of the highest and steepest premier crus in Gevrey. Thin soil over limestone and scree.
appellations.nerd_note: Fourrier's Goulots is often the most austere of its premier crus in youth and one of the slowest to open; the site's narrow shape is the likely origin of the name (*goulot*, a bottleneck).

appellations.name: Gevrey-Chambertin premier cru Petite Chapelle
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary:
Petite Chapelle sits directly below Chapelle-Chambertin, at 4.0 ha, on the lower slope toward the Route des Grands Crus. The chapel in both names was built by the monks of the Abbey of Bèze in 1155 and pulled down after the Revolution. The wine is plump and perfumed, a softer, more accessible cousin of the grand cru above.

It is one of the cluster of premier crus pressed against the grands crus on the Route des Grands Crus side of Gevrey, with Cherbaudes to the north and En Ergot to the south. Its deeper soil gives a rounder, earlier wine than Chapelle-Chambertin itself, but the family likeness is clear: red cherry, spice and a supple, perfumed texture.
appellations.terroir: East-southeast-facing at about 260 m, almost flat, on deep brown limestone-clay.
appellations.nerd_note: Petite Chapelle is sometimes labelled 'Champitonnois', the old name of the lieu-dit.

appellations.name: Gevrey-Chambertin premier cru Petits Cazetiers
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: A 0.94 ha strip on the edge of Les Cazetiers, at the northern end of the Côte Saint-Jacques. It shares the same soils and gives a slightly lighter, more immediate version of the Cazetiers style: dark cherry, spice and a firm, fresh finish.
appellations.terroir: East-southeast-facing at 305 to 330 m on stony brown limestone, between Les Cazetiers and Combe au Moine.
appellations.nerd_note: Few growers bottle it separately; the name is often folded into a Gevrey premier cru blend.

appellations.name: Gevrey-Chambertin premier cru Poissenot
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: Poissenot is a steep 2.2 ha premier cru above the Clos des Varoilles, at the edge of the woods in the Combe de Lavaux. It makes a fine-boned, fresh Gevrey with red fruit and a mineral edge, and Humbert Frères' version is the reference.
appellations.terroir: Very steep, south-southeast-facing at 325 to 395 m, slope around 29%. Thin, stony limestone soils.
appellations.nerd_note: It is one of the highest premier crus in the Côte de Nuits, touching 390 m at its upper edge.

The Clos Salomon is a 7.0 ha walled Givry premier cru, a monopole of Domaine du Clos Salomon. Its red is supple and red-fruited, one of Givry's most elegant.

The clos sits on the gentle slope beside the Clos Saint-Paul and Les Grands Prétans, on limestone and marl.

appellations.name: Givry premier cru Clos du Cellier aux Moines
match: Givry premier cru Clos du Cellier aux Moines
Givry 1er Cru Clos du Cellier aux Moines
Givry Premier Cru Clos du Cellier aux Moines
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir for red; Chardonnay for white
appellations.summary:
The Clos du Cellier aux Moines is the most famous premier cru of Givry and one of the oldest walled vineyards of the Côte Chalonnaise. It was planted by Cistercian monks of the Abbey of La Ferté in the 12th century, and their cellar, the *cellier* of the name, still stands at the top of the slope. At 13.3 ha it faces south-southwest on a steep hillside above the village, unusual for Burgundy.

Its reds are the most structured of Givry: dark cherry, spice and firm tannin, with a mineral freshness. The legend that Givry was Henri IV's favourite wine is often told here, though it is probably apocryphal. Domaine du Cellier aux Moines, bought by Philippe Pascal in 2004, and Domaine Joblot are the main producers.
appellations.terroir: South-southwest-facing at 240 to 310 m, steep. Thin limestone soils with marl over Jurassic limestone, unusually stony for the Côte Chalonnaise.
appellations.nerd_note: The south-southwest exposure gives more afternoon sun than most Côte d'Or premiers crus, which suits this cooler, more southerly hill country.

The Clos Charlé lies below it, and its limestone and marl give firm, red-fruited wines.

appellations.nerd_note: The grand cru Corton Hautes Mourottes lies alongside, on almost identical ground.

appellations.terroir: Gentle south slope at 245 to 270 m, on brown limestone-clay with gravel.
appellations.nerd_note: *Corvée* refers to the unpaid labour tenants owed their lord, a common climat name across the Côte.

La Fussière is the largest premier cru of the Maranges, a 42.6 ha south-facing slope across Dezize-lès-Maranges and Cheilly-lès-Maranges, at the southern tip of the Côte de Beaune. Its reds are the deepest of the appellation: dark-fruited, firm and earthy, good value Côte de Beaune.

Les Clos Roussots and Le Clos des Loyères lie below it. Bachelet-Monnot's version is a reference.

appellations.nerd_note: The Maranges appellation was created in 1989 from three villages that had sold their wine as Côte de Beaune-Villages.

Mercurey Premier Cru Clos des Myglands
appellations.grapes: Pinot Noir for red; Chardonnay for white
appellations.summary:
The Clos des Myglands is a 6.3 ha monopole of Domaine Faiveley, the largest landowner in Mercurey. Mercurey is the biggest appellation of the Côte Chalonnaise and mostly red, and the Clos des Myglands is one of its most consistent reds: supple, red-fruited and firm, a Burgundy of real class at a modest price.

It sits on the gentle slope beside the Clos l'Evêque, and Faiveley's red is one of the best-value Burgundies from a top house.
appellations.terroir: East-southeast-facing at 255 to 270 m, gentle slope, limestone and marl. The gradient is gentle, about 8%, and the soil a mix of limestone and marl typical of the northern Côte Chalonnaise.
appellations.nerd_note: Faiveley has owned vineyards in Mercurey since the 1930s and is the appellation's biggest landowner.
